**Abstract.** For the planar density equal to one on a horizontal strip and to a constant \(\lambda>1\) outside it, every member of the explicit symmetric four-arc family has a three-arc competitor of exactly the same weighted area and strictly smaller weighted perimeter. We prove the quantitative improvement \(\gamma_\lambda/h\), including the curvature endpoint \(h=1\). The argument compares \(P-hA\) at equal curvature, then selects the greatest equal-area root. Coordinate constructions and integral identities justify the geometric comparison independently of any classification of minimizers.

## 1. Introduction and statement

Cañete, Miranda Jr. and Vittone [1, §3.2] studied the isoperimetric problem for a plane whose density jumps across the boundary of a strip. Their Lemma 3.8 and Proposition 3.9 reduce the possible minimizers, up to density-preserving isometries, to four families with vertical reflection symmetry: disks contained in the strip, stadiums with straight sides on the interfaces, three-arc regions with a bottom segment, and four-arc regions with congruent exterior caps. Their Conjecture 3.12 predicts the exclusion of the last family. We give the corrected elementary comparison of the supplied note by Skilyn Leon, Rosa Pavlak, Evelyn Pulla and Xi Sisi Shen [2]. The comparison is self-contained for its explicit regions; its implication for the unrestricted conjecture uses the external classification and is discussed in Section 6.

Fix a real number \(\lambda>1\). The density and the geometric quantities used throughout are
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_\lambda(x,y)&=\begin{cases}1,&|y|\leq1,\\ \lambda,&|y|>1,\end{cases}\\
A_\lambda(F)&=\int_F f_\lambda\,dx\,dy,
& P_\lambda(F)&=\int_{\partial F}f_\lambda\,d\mathcal H^1.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(1.1)}
\]
Here \(\mathcal H^1\) is Euclidean one-dimensional Hausdorff measure and \(\partial F\) is the complete topological boundary. In particular, the density is one on both interfaces \(|y|=1\). The regions constructed below are closed and bounded, and both integrals are finite. [@lean:StripDensity] [@lean:WeightedArea] [@lean:FrontierMeasure] [@lean:WeightedPerimeter]

Write
\[
\gamma_\lambda=\lambda\arccos(1/\lambda)-\sqrt{1-\lambda^{-2}}.
\qquad\mathrm{(1.2)}
\]
The four-arc region \(C_h\) has common circular radius \(h^{-1}\), where \(0<h\leq1\), and exterior half-angle \(\alpha=\arccos(h/\lambda)\). Thus \(\lambda\cos\alpha=h\). Its exact coordinate definition, and that of the three-arc family \(E_s\), are given in Section 2. [@lean:CMVElementary.gamma] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.fourCandidate_snell]

**Theorem 1 (geometric comparison).** *For every real \(\lambda>1\), one has \(\gamma_\lambda>0\). For every real \(h\) with \(0<h\leq1\), there exists a real \(r\) with \(0<r<h\) such that*
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_\lambda(E_r)&=A_\lambda(C_h),\\
P_\lambda(C_h)-P_\lambda(E_r)&>\frac{\gamma_\lambda}{h}>0.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(1.3)}
\]
*Consequently, \(C_h\) does not minimize weighted perimeter at its weighted area.* [@lean:CMVElementary.geometric_comparison]

In both statements of Theorem 1 in [2], including its display (3.2), the expression on the left must be \(P_\lambda(C_h)-P_\lambda(E_r)\), as in (1.3), not \(A_\lambda(C_h)-P_\lambda(E_r)\). The latter is false. The original note is retained unchanged as a source and style reference; its literal erroneous displays are not the result proved here.

## 2. Coordinate regions and geometric formulas

For \(-1\leq z\leq1\), set
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(z)&=\lambda\arccos(z/\lambda)+\arcsin z,\\
D(z)&=\sqrt{1-z^2/\lambda^2}-\sqrt{1-z^2}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.1)}
\]
The dependence on \(\lambda\) is suppressed. Notice that \(D(z)\geq0\): the first radicand is at least the second. For \(0<s\leq1\), put \(q=2s-1\) and define
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_3(s)&=\frac{B(q)+\pi/2+(2s+1)D(q)}{s^2},
& P_3(s)&=\frac{2\bigl(B(q)+\pi/2+D(q)\bigr)}{s},\\
A_4(s)&=\frac{2\bigl(B(s)+sD(s)\bigr)}{s^2},
& P_4(s)&=\frac{4B(s)}{s}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.2)}
\]
The values \(A_3(1)\) and \(P_3(1)\) are scalar endpoint values only; the geometric competitors have parameter strictly less than one. [@lean:CMVElementary.B] [@lean:CMVElementary.D] [@lean:CMVElementary.D_nonneg] [@lean:CMVElementary.A3] [@lean:CMVElementary.P3] [@lean:CMVElementary.A4] [@lean:CMVElementary.P4]

For \(0<h\leq1\), let \(R=h^{-1}\), \(\alpha=\arccos(h/\lambda)\) and \(d=D(h)/h\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
K_h&=\{(x,y):-1\leq y\leq1,\ |x|\leq d+\sqrt{R^2-y^2}\},\\
H_h&=\{(x,y):y\geq1,\ x^2+(y-(1-R\cos\alpha))^2\leq R^2\},\\
\sigma(x,y)&=(x,-y),\qquad C_h=K_h\cup H_h\cup\sigma(H_h).
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.3)}
\]
Reflection \(\sigma\) supplies the lower cap. Its non-endpoint exterior arc lies in \(y<-1\), not merely in \(y<1\). Both \(C_h\) and the three-arc region below are symmetric about the vertical axis; \(C_h\) additionally has horizontal reflection symmetry. [@lean:CMVElementary.K] [@lean:CMVElementary.upperCap4] [@lean:CMVElementary.sigma] [@lean:CMVElementary.C]

For \(0<s<1\), now let \(q=2s-1\), \(R=s^{-1}\), \(\alpha=\arccos(q/\lambda)\), and \(b=D(q)/s\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
K_s^{(3)}&=\{(x,y):-1\leq y\leq1,\ |x|\leq b+\sqrt{R^2-(y-(R-1))^2}\},\\
H_s^{(3)}&=\{(x,y):y\geq1,\ x^2+(y-(1-R\cos\alpha))^2\leq R^2\},\\
E_s&=K_s^{(3)}\cup H_s^{(3)}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.4)}
\]
Because \(R>1\), the strip radicand is nonnegative. Since \(b\geq0\), every horizontal section is an interval. The cap is defined as a disk intersected with a half-plane, so its definition does not discard the major-segment branch. [@lean:CMVElementary.K3] [@lean:CMVElementary.upperCap3] [@lean:CMVElementary.E] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.K3_core]

**Proposition 1 (geometric realization).** *For every \(\lambda>1\), the regions \(C_h\), \(0<h\leq1\), and \(E_s\), \(0<s<1\), are closed, bounded and measurable. Their densities are integrable over the regions and their complete frontiers, whose Euclidean lengths are finite. They satisfy*
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_\lambda(C_h)&=A_4(h),&P_\lambda(C_h)&=P_4(h),\\
A_\lambda(E_s)&=A_3(s),&P_\lambda(E_s)&=P_3(s).
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.5)}
\]
*The open attaching chords are interior to the unions. The bottom frontier of \(E_s\) is exactly the segment \(\{(x,-1):|x|\leq b\}\). For \(s<1/2\), its exterior cap has half-angle greater than \(\pi/2\); for \(s=1/2\), the region is the disk of radius two centered at \((0,1)\).* [@lean:CMVElementary.geometric_realization]

*Proof.* At \(y=\pm1\), the half-width in (2.3) is
\[
d+\sqrt{R^2-1}
=\frac{D(h)+\sqrt{1-h^2}}{h}
=\frac{\sin\alpha}{h}.
\]
Thus the cap and core chords agree. At a strict interior point of either chord the disk inequalities are strict on the appropriate sides of the interface, giving a neighborhood inside their union. The exposed frontier consists precisely of the two strip arcs and the two exterior arcs. Their intersections are confined to the four junctions and hence have zero \(\mathcal H^1\)-measure. The strip arcs have total length \(4\arcsin(h)/h\); the exterior arcs have total length \(4\alpha/h\). It follows that
\[
P_\lambda(C_h)=\frac{4\arcsin h+4\lambda\alpha}{h}=P_4(h).
\qquad\mathrm{(2.6)}
\]
These are lengths of the actual frontier, not independently assigned boundary data. [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.four_upper_chord] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.four_lower_chord] [@lean:FourArcAssembly.frontier_carrier] [@lean:fourArc_frontier_weightedPerimeter_eq]

Horizontal integration gives the central area and the area of one cap:
\[
\begin{aligned}
|K_h|&=\frac{4D(h)}h+\frac{2\sqrt{1-h^2}}h+\frac{2\arcsin h}{h^2},\\
|H_h|&=\frac{\alpha-\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{h^2}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.7)}
\]
The overlaps are contained in the interface lines and have zero planar area. Adding the central area and twice the weighted cap area, then using \(\lambda\cos\alpha=h\), gives \(A_\lambda(C_h)=A_4(h)\). The formulas remain valid at \(h=1\). [@lean:FourArcAssembly.weightedArea_formula] [@lean:FourArcCandidate.candidate_area_formula] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.C_area]

For (2.4), the upper half-width is
\[
b+\frac{\sqrt{1-q^2}}s=\frac{\sin\alpha}s.
\]
The strict attaching chord is again interior to the union. At \(y=-1\), the radicand vanishes; the whole segment of length \(2b\) remains exposed and has density one. Each of the two strip arcs has central angle \(\arcsin q+\pi/2\), and the exterior arc has central angle \(2\alpha\). Therefore
\[
P_\lambda(E_s)
=\frac{2(\arcsin q+\pi/2)+2\lambda\alpha}{s}+2b
=P_3(s).
\qquad\mathrm{(2.8)}
\]
No attaching chord contributes to this perimeter. [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.three_strict_chord] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.E_bottom_frontier] [@lean:TypeThreeAssembly.frontier_carrier] [@lean:TypeThreeAssembly.weightedPerimeter_formula]

The corresponding area calculation is
\[
\begin{aligned}
|K_s^{(3)}|&=\frac{4D(q)}s+
\frac{\arcsin q+\pi/2+q\sqrt{1-q^2}}{s^2},\\
\lambda|H_s^{(3)}|&=\frac{\lambda\alpha-q\sin\alpha}{s^2}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(2.9)}
\]
Their sum is \(A_3(s)\). The cap formula follows by integrating the disk sections and holds throughout \(0<\alpha<\pi\), including \(\alpha>\pi/2\). When \(s=1/2\), one has \(q=b=0\), \(R=2\) and \(\alpha=\pi/2\); the three circle centers coincide at \((0,1)\), and the bottom segment reduces to \((0,-1)\). Thus
\[
E_{1/2}=\{(x,y):x^2+(y-1)^2\leq4\}.
\qquad\mathrm{(2.10)}
\]
This is a disk, not a pinched region. [@lean:volume_upper_circular_segment] [@lean:TypeThreeAssembly.core_weightedArea_formula] [@lean:TypeThreeAssembly.weightedArea_formula] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.E_half_disk]

For completeness, the coordinate formulas in (2.3) and (2.4) are identified exactly with the cap-and-core constructions used to prove the area and frontier formulas. Their closedness follows from the coordinate inequalities, and boundedness from their finite rectangle-and-disk decompositions. Each frontier is a finite union of circular arcs and, for \(E_s\), the bottom segment. Exact arc-length formulas give finite frontier measure; boundedness of the density then gives both integrability assertions. Thus (2.5) consists of proved integral identities for specified sets, not assumptions supplied to the comparison. \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.C_assembly] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.E_assembly] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.four_regularity] [@lean:CMVElementary.GeometryBridge.three_regularity]

## 3. Two comparisons at the same curvature

Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(z)&=B(z)-zD(z),\\
J(u)&=2S(u)-S(2u-1)-\pi/2,\\
j(u)&=4\bigl(D(2u-1)-D(u)\bigr),\qquad H(u)=J(u)-uj(u).
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.1)}
\]
Here \(0\leq u\leq1\). We write \(j\) for the continuous extension of \(J'\); it is defined by the displayed formula even at the endpoints, where no differentiation is intended. [@lean:CMVElementary.S] [@lean:CMVElementary.J] [@lean:CMVElementary.jprime] [@lean:CMVElementary.H]

**Lemma 1.** *For \(\lambda>1\) and \(0\leq u\leq1\),*
\[
J(u)\geq\gamma_\lambda>0,\qquad H(u)\geq\gamma_\lambda.
\qquad\mathrm{(3.2)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.J_lower] [@lean:CMVElementary.H_lower] [@lean:CMVElementary.gamma_pos]

*Proof.* The elementary normalization
\[
\frac{\sqrt{\lambda^2-z^2}}\lambda=\sqrt{1-z^2/\lambda^2}
\qquad(\lambda>0)
\]
identifies (2.1) with the radical normalization used in the underlying calculus. For \(-1<z<1\), differentiation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D'(z)&=z\left(\frac1{\sqrt{1-z^2}}-
\frac1{\lambda\sqrt{\lambda^2-z^2}}\right),\\
B'(z)+D(z)&=zD'(z),\qquad S'(z)=-2D(z).
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.3)}
\]
The coefficient of \(z\) in \(D'(z)\) is positive, since \(\lambda\sqrt{\lambda^2-z^2}>\sqrt{1-z^2}>0\). Consequently \(D\) is even and strictly increasing on \([0,1]\), with endpoint continuity supplying the closed interval. [@lean:CMVElementary.DerivativePilot.sqrt_normalization] [@lean:CMVElementary.DerivativePilot.hasDerivAt_D] [@lean:CMVElementary.hasDerivAt_S] [@lean:CMVElementary.D_even] [@lean:CMVElementary.D_strictMono]

The inverse trigonometric reflection identities yield
\[
S(-z)=\lambda\pi-S(z),\qquad
J(0)=J(1)=S(1)-\pi/2=\gamma_\lambda.
\qquad\mathrm{(3.4)}
\]
To prove positivity, put \(\theta=\arccos(1/\lambda)\in(0,\pi/2)\). Then \(\gamma_\lambda=\lambda\theta-\sin\theta>0\), since \(\sin\theta\leq\theta<\lambda\theta\). On \((0,1)\), (3.3) gives \(J'=j\). Evenness and strict increase of \(D\) show that
\[
j(u)\begin{cases}>0,&0<u<1/3,\\=0,&u=1/3,\\<0,&1/3<u<1.\end{cases}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.5)}
\]
Indeed, compare \(|2u-1|\) with \(u\). Thus \(J\) increases to \(1/3\) and decreases thereafter, proving its lower bound from the equal endpoint values. On \([1/3,1]\), one also has \(j\leq0\), so \(H\geq J\). [@lean:CMVElementary.S_reflection] [@lean:CMVElementary.DerivativePilot.J_zero] [@lean:CMVElementary.J_one] [@lean:CMVElementary.hasDerivAt_J] [@lean:CMVElementary.jprime_pos] [@lean:CMVElementary.jprime_neg] [@lean:CMVElementary.H_ge_J]

It remains to consider \(0<u\leq1/3\). By evenness,
\[
j(t)=4\bigl(D(1-2t)-D(t)\bigr),\qquad 0\leq t\leq1/3.
\]
As \(t\) increases, the first argument decreases and the second increases. Hence \(j\) is nonincreasing on this closed interval. The mean value theorem, applied to \(J\) on \([0,u]\), supplies \(c\in(0,u)\) with
\[
J(u)-J(0)=u j(c)\geq u j(u).
\qquad\mathrm{(3.6)}
\]
Therefore \(H(u)\geq J(0)=\gamma_\lambda\). At \(u=0\) the result is immediate. This is the decreasing-derivative tangent argument used for the formal lower bound: the left endpoint lies below the tangent at the right endpoint. It requires continuity of \(J\) at zero, not differentiation there. \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.MonotoneTangent.jprime_antitone_lower_third] [@lean:CMVElementary.MonotoneTangent.endpoint_tangent] [@lean:CMVElementary.MonotoneTangent.h_lower_third_of_monotone_tangent]

The tangent argument is the same concavity mechanism as in [2]. The formal development also establishes, separately, all of the derivative and limit identities appearing there:
\[
\begin{aligned}
j'(u)&=8D'(2u-1)-4D'(u)<0,\\
H'(u)&=-u j'(u)>0\qquad(0<u<1/3),\\
\lim_{u\downarrow0}H(u)&=\gamma_\lambda.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.7)}
\]
The signs follow because \(2u-1<0<u\). These facts justify the alternative proof by increasing \(H\) from its limit, but that is not the lemma chain used to prove the lower-third bound above. All endpoint values of \(j\) and \(H\) are continuous extensions; no derivative of a square root at its endpoint is used. [@lean:CMVElementary.auxiliary_claims]

**Proposition 2 (same-curvature comparisons).** *For \(\lambda>1\) and \(0<h\leq1\),*
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_4(h)-A_3(h)&\geq\frac{\gamma_\lambda}{h^2}>0,\\
\bigl(P_4(h)-hA_4(h)\bigr)-\bigl(P_3(h)-hA_3(h)\bigr)
&\geq\frac{\gamma_\lambda}{h}>0.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.8)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.same_curvature_claims]

*Proof.* Substitution into (2.2), with \(q=2h-1\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
h\bigl(P_4(h)-hA_4(h)\bigr)&=2S(h),\\
h\bigl(P_3(h)-hA_3(h)\bigr)&=S(q)+\pi/2,\\
h^2\bigl(A_4(h)-A_3(h)\bigr)&=J(h)-hj(h)=H(h).
\end{aligned}
\qquad\mathrm{(3.9)}
\]
Subtract the first two identities and apply Lemma 1; the last identity gives the area inequality. Division by the positive quantities \(h\) and \(h^2\) proves (3.8). \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.support_identity] [@lean:CMVElementary.area_identity]

## 4. Variation and the greatest equal-area root

**Lemma 2.** *For \(\lambda>1\), the functions \(A_3\) and \(P_3\) are continuous on \((0,1]\), differentiable on \((0,1)\), and satisfy*
\[
P_3'(s)=sA_3'(s)\quad(0<s<1),\qquad
\lim_{s\downarrow0}A_3(s)=+\infty.
\qquad\mathrm{(4.1)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.three_arc_calculus_claims]

*Proof.* Continuity follows from (2.1)–(2.2). On the open interval all differentiated radicals have positive arguments. With \(q=2s-1\), write
\[
\begin{aligned}
N(s)&=B(q)+\pi/2+(2s+1)D(q),\\
M(s)&=2\bigl(B(q)+\pi/2+D(q)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Then \(A_3=N/s^2\) and \(P_3=M/s\). By (3.3),
\[
N'(s)=8sD'(q),\qquad M'(s)=8sD'(q)-4D(q),\qquad
2N(s)-M(s)=4sD(q).
\]
The quotient rule now gives
\[
s^2\bigl(P_3'(s)-sA_3'(s)\bigr)
=s\bigl(M'(s)-N'(s)\bigr)+2N(s)-M(s)=0.
\]
The reused calculus formulas are identified with (2.2) by the positive-\(\lambda\) radical normalization, so they give precisely this variational identity, not a different family. [@lean:CMVElementary.scalar_identification_claims] [@lean:CMVElementary.three_arc_variational_hasDerivAt]

Finally, as \(s\downarrow0\), the numerator \(N(s)\) tends to
\[
B(-1)+\pi/2+D(-1)
=\lambda\arccos(-1/\lambda)+\sqrt{1-\lambda^{-2}}>0.
\]
Division by \(s^2\downarrow0\) proves the divergence. \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.A3_tendsto_atRight_zero]

**Lemma 3 (greatest equal-area root).** *Let \(\lambda>1\) and \(0<h\leq1\), and put \(V=A_4(h)\). There exist \(0<\varepsilon<r<h\) such that the set*
\[
Z=\{s\in[\varepsilon,h]:A_3(s)=V\}
\qquad\mathrm{(4.2)}
\]
*is nonempty and compact, \(r=\max Z\), and*
\[
A_3(r)=V,\qquad A_3(s)<V\quad(r<s\leq h).
\qquad\mathrm{(4.3)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.Z] [@lean:CMVElementary.greatest_root_claims]

*Proof.* Proposition 2 gives \(A_3(h)<V\). By Lemma 2, choose \(0<\varepsilon<h\) with \(A_3(\varepsilon)>V\). The intermediate value theorem gives a point of \(Z\). Continuity makes \(Z\) a closed subset of the compact interval \([\varepsilon,h]\), so it has a greatest element \(r\). The strict endpoint inequalities give \(\varepsilon<r<h\). If \(r<s\leq h\) and \(A_3(s)=V\), maximality fails. If \(A_3(s)>V\), continuity between \(s\) and \(h\) gives a later equal-area root, again a contradiction. This proves (4.3). No root uniqueness or global monotonicity of \(A_3\) has been assumed. \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.exists_greatest_level_root]

## 5. The equal-area perimeter comparison

**Theorem 2 (scalar comparison).** *For every \(\lambda>1\), one has \(\gamma_\lambda>0\); for every \(0<h\leq1\), there exists \(0<r<h\) such that*
\[
A_3(r)=A_4(h),\qquad P_4(h)-P_3(r)>\frac{\gamma_\lambda}{h}>0.
\qquad\mathrm{(5.1)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.scalar_comparison]

*Proof.* Choose the greatest root from Lemma 3 and define
\[
Q(s)=P_3(s)+s\bigl(V-A_3(s)\bigr),\qquad r\leq s\leq h.
\qquad\mathrm{(5.2)}
\]
This function is continuous on \([r,h]\). On its interior, Lemma 2 and the strict area barrier give
\[
Q'(s)=P_3'(s)+V-A_3(s)-sA_3'(s)=V-A_3(s)>0.
\qquad\mathrm{(5.3)}
\]
The mean value theorem therefore gives the strict comparison
\[
P_3(r)=Q(r)<Q(h)=P_3(h)+h\bigl(A_4(h)-A_3(h)\bigr).
\qquad\mathrm{(5.4)}
\]
[@lean:CMVElementary.Q] [@lean:CMVElementary.strict_support_comparison] [@lean:CMVElementary.greatest_root_claims]

Subtracting (5.4) from \(P_4(h)\) and using Proposition 2 yields
\[
P_4(h)-P_3(r)>\frac{\gamma_\lambda}{h}>0.
\qquad\mathrm{(5.5)}
\]
This proves the scalar theorem. The complete elementary route consists of the auxiliary bounds, the two same-curvature identities, the variational calculus and its formula identifications, and this greatest-root construction with the strict \(Q\) comparison; all follow from \(\lambda>1\). \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.elementary_route]

*Proof of Theorem 1.* The root in Theorem 2 satisfies \(0<r<h\leq1\), hence \(r<1\). Proposition 1 applies to \(C_h\) and \(E_r\). Substituting their actual area and perimeter identities into (5.1) gives (1.3), with exact equality of weighted areas and a strictly positive perimeter improvement. \(\square\) [@lean:CMVElementary.geometric_comparison]

## 6. Endpoints and scope

The endpoint \(h=1\) causes no loss: the four-arc coordinate construction remains valid, the scalar formulas are continuous at one, and differentiation in the final comparison takes place only on \((r,h)\). The competitor remains strictly inside the three-arc parameter interval. Major caps and the radius-two disk are already included in Proposition 1. The choice of a greatest root, rather than a presumed unique root, is essential to the stated argument.

The improvement is positive for every fixed \(\lambda>1\), but no positive margin uniform as \(\lambda\downarrow1\) is claimed. Formula (1.2) gives \(\gamma_\lambda\to0\). Thus the phrase “for every density contrast” does not mean a density-independent lower bound.

**Corollary (informal; using the external classification).** *For each \(\lambda>1\), there is a transition area \(v_0>\pi\) with the ball, stadium and three-arc alternatives of [1, Conjecture 3.12]. For \(0<v<\pi\), minimizers are disks contained in the strip; for \(\pi<v<v_0\), they are stadiums; for \(v>v_0\), they are three-arc regions. At \(v=\pi\) the stadium degenerates to a disk. At \(v=v_0\), stadium and three-arc minimizers coexist. The classification is up to density-preserving isometries and the relevant measure equivalence; no uniqueness is asserted.*

*Proof using [1].* Proposition 3.9 supplies vertical reflection symmetry for arbitrary minimizers. Lemma 3.8 then supplies its four candidate families; Step 2 of its proof gives horizontal symmetry of the four-arc family, placing that family, after a density-preserving isometry, in the form \(C_h\). Theorem 1 excludes it. Theorem 3.16 of [1] supplies the remaining area ranges and transition coexistence, so its residual four-arc alternative disappears. \(\square\)

This corollary uses a further measure-theoretic transfer. For the explicit finite piecewise-circular Jordan regions here, the complete and reduced boundaries agree up to an \(\mathcal H^1\)-null set, so their weighted boundary integrals agree, including the density-one interfaces. This agreement was already stated in [2, §3]; it was not omitted from that draft. For an arbitrary minimizer, one must first invoke the external regular-representative and classification results. Reduced-boundary perimeter is insensitive to changes on sets of planar measure zero; complete-frontier perimeter need not be. Accordingly, [2]'s broad conjecture claim is justified as the cited corollary, while its final explicit-family scope remark describes the self-contained theorem.

The Lean-verified results are the explicit geometric comparison, the separately named scalar comparison, the elementary route, and the unconditional geometric realization. The six frozen lower-level modules supply calculus, circular geometry, and integral/frontier infrastructure, not an earlier final exclusion theorem. Neither the external classification nor the bounded-variation and reduced-boundary transfer is formalized or introduced as an extra axiom. Exhaustive declaration mappings, source code, and retained verification evidence belong to the supplement rather than the mathematical argument.

## References

[1] Antonio Cañete, Michele Miranda Jr. and Davide Vittone, *Some isoperimetric problems in planes with density*, Journal of Geometric Analysis **20** (2010), 243–290. Preprint arXiv:0906.1256. In particular, §2, Lemma 3.8, Proposition 3.9, Conjecture 3.12 and Theorem 3.16.

[2] Skilyn Leon, Rosa Pavlak, Evelyn Pulla and Xi Sisi Shen, *An elementary comparison for four-arc regions in a planar strip density*, supplied undated note, `CMV_Strip_Density_Problem.pdf`, §§3–6 and Remarks 1–3; the two printed Theorem 1 inequalities are corrected in (1.3).

classifications.informal_statement: The extended Euclidean distance between the realized endpoints of a horizontal segment equals its positive scalar length \(L\), embedded in the nonnegative extended reals.
classifications.latex_explanation: The endpoints have equal vertical coordinates and horizontal separation \(L\).

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean \(\mathcal H^1\)-measure of a horizontal segment carrier equals its scalar length \(L\).
classifications.latex_explanation: Identify it with the affine segment and use the endpoint-distance formula for the measure of a segment.

classifications.informal_statement: For every cap, the image of its coordinate arclength parametrization on \([-R\theta,R\theta]\) is exactly its selected arc trace.
classifications.latex_explanation: The forward inclusion follows from the circle and half-plane identities. Inverse trigonometric reconstruction gives a parameter for every trace point, including major-arc points.

classifications.informal_statement: The realized cap parameter image on its closed parameter interval equals the Euclidean image of the cap arc trace.
classifications.latex_explanation: Transport the preceding set equality through the coordinate homeomorphism.

classifications.informal_statement: For every cap, the Euclidean \(\mathcal H^1\)-measure of its selected arc trace equals its scalar arc length.
classifications.latex_explanation: Combine the exact parameter-image identity and the exact Hausdorff length of the realized parametrization.

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean image of the left exposed strip-core arc is measurable.
classifications.latex_explanation: The realized continuous parametrization has a compact interval domain, so its image is compact and Borel measurable.

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean image of the right exposed strip-core arc is measurable.
classifications.latex_explanation: The realized continuous parametrization has a compact interval domain, so its image is compact and Borel measurable.

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean image of every cap arc trace is measurable.
classifications.latex_explanation: It is a continuous image of a compact interval in a Hausdorff space, hence compact and Borel measurable.

classifications.informal_statement: For four planar sets \(A,B,C,D\), define the union of the six pairwise intersections.
classifications.latex_explanation: This single set records all possible overlap errors in four-component perimeter additivity.
These are the possible four-arc junctions at the two interfaces; repeated points are harmless.

classifications.informal_statement: For every four-arc assembly, the union of pairwise intersections of its four arc traces is contained in the junction set for its core chord.
classifications.latex_explanation: The trace inequalities and circle equations restrict any shared point to an attaching endpoint.

classifications.informal_statement: For every real \(L\), the junction set is finite.
classifications.latex_explanation: It is explicitly a set of at most four points.

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean junction set is the coordinate homeomorphism image of the planar junction set.
classifications.latex_explanation: It has identical point coordinates and is used with Euclidean Hausdorff measure.

classifications.informal_statement: The Euclidean junction set is finite for every real chord parameter.
classifications.latex_explanation: Images of finite sets are finite.

classifications.informal_statement: Every Euclidean junction set has zero one-dimensional Hausdorff measure.
classifications.latex_explanation: Finite sets have zero Hausdorff measure in positive dimension.

classifications.informal_statement: For every four-arc assembly, the Euclidean image of the union of pairwise arc-trace intersections has zero \(\mathcal H^1\)-measure.
classifications.latex_explanation: It is contained in the null finite junction set; this establishes the needed almost-everywhere disjointness.

classifications.informal_statement: The frontier of a four-arc carrier in its Euclidean realization is exactly the union of the Euclidean images of its two core arcs and two cap arcs.
classifications.latex_explanation: A homeomorphism transports the proved coordinate frontier decomposition without adding hidden chord components.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the Euclidean density as the coordinate density composed with the inverse coordinate homeomorphism.
classifications.latex_explanation: It has the same values at the same coordinates, with Euclidean measure semantics.

classifications.informal_statement:
For any real \(\lambda\) and Euclidean set \(S\) with
\[
\mathcal H^1(S)<\infty,
\]
the Euclidean strip density is integrable over \(S\) against \(\mathcal H^1\).
classifications.latex_explanation: Measurability and a global finite bound on the piecewise constant density give integrability on finite measure sets.

classifications.informal_statement:
For real \(\lambda\) and an upper cap based on
\[
y=1,
\]
the integral of Euclidean strip density over its actual arc trace against \(\mathcal H^1\) equals \(\lambda\) times its arc length.
classifications.latex_explanation: Density is \(\lambda\) away from the two null endpoints; the trace has exactly the proved circular arc length.

classifications.informal_statement:
Let \(A,B,C,D\) be Euclidean sets whose six pairwise intersections are
\[
\mathcal H^1
\]
-null, with \(B,C,D\) measurable. If a real function is integrable on each of the four sets against
\[
\mathcal H^1,
\]
its integral over
\[
A\cup(B\cup(C\cup D))
\]
equals the sum of the four integrals.
classifications.latex_explanation: Repeated two-set integral additivity applies under almost-everywhere disjointness. The statement does not require a separately supplied measurability hypothesis on \(A\).

classifications.informal_statement: For four subsets \(A,B,C,D\) of any type, define the union of their six pairwise intersections.
classifications.latex_explanation: Despite its name, this is a generic set expression; it is instantiated in the Euclidean plane for measure arguments.

classifications.informal_statement: If the union of six pairwise intersections of four Euclidean sets has zero \(\mathcal H^1\)-measure, then every pair of those sets is almost-everywhere disjoint for that measure.
classifications.latex_explanation: Each intersection is contained in the null union, so monotonicity of measure proves the six assertions.

classifications.informal_statement: For every real \(\lambda\) and four-arc assembly, its auxiliary parametrized weighted perimeter equals the density integral against the canonical complete-frontier measure of its carrier.
classifications.latex_explanation: The exact frontier decomposition, exact Euclidean arc lengths, branchwise density integrals and null overlaps identify the actual perimeter. This theorem removes the possibility of freely assigning perimeter data.

classifications.informal_statement:
Let \(a<b\), let
\[
F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R
\]
be continuous on \([a,b]\), and suppose
\[
F(a)>V>F(b).
\]
There exists \(r\in(a,b)\) with
\[
F(r)=V,
\]
greatest in \([a,b]\cap F^{-1}(\{V\})\), and
\[
F(t)<V
\]
for \(r<t\leq b\).
classifications.latex_explanation: The intermediate value theorem supplies a level point; the closed level set in a compact interval has a greatest point. A later value at or above the level would give a later root, contradicting maximality.

classifications.informal_statement:
Let \(a<b\). Suppose \(A,P\) are continuous on \([a,b]\),
\[
A(a)=V,
\]
and
\[
A(t)<V
\]
on \((a,b)\). Suppose also that for every interior \(t\), there is a real \(d\) with
\[
A'(t)=d
\]
and
\[
P'(t)=td,
\]
both derivatives existing. Then
\[
P(a)<P(b)+b[V-A(b)].
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
The continuous function
\[
Q(t)=P(t)+t[V-A(t)]
\]
has derivative
\[
V-A(t)>0
\]
in the interior and is strictly increasing on the closed interval. No endpoint differentiability is needed.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the three-arc shape parameter
\[
q(h)=2h-1
\]
for real \(h\).
classifications.latex_explanation: This affine parameter is the cosine of the inner angle in the geometric assembly.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the angle combination
\[
\lambda\arccos(q(h)/\lambda)+\arcsin(q(h)).
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: It is the article's \(B(q(h))\), with the density argument explicitly retained.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
\delta_3(h)=\sqrt{\lambda^2-q(h)^2}/\lambda-\sqrt{1-q(h)^2}.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: For positive density, radical normalization identifies this with \(D(q(h))\); it is the width correction in the three-arc scalar formulas.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the normalized three-arc scalar area
\[
[B(q(h))+\pi/2+(q(h)+2)\delta_3(h)]/h^2.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: Once the positive-density radical identity is proved, this is precisely \(A_3(h)\); total definitions alone do not impose a geometric domain.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the normalized three-arc scalar perimeter
\[
2[B(q(h))+\pi/2+\delta_3(h)]/h.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The identification with \(P_3(h)\) uses the same radical normalization and includes the bottom-segment term.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the four-arc angle combination
\[
\lambda\arccos(h/\lambda)+\arcsin h.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This is exactly the article's \(B(h)\).

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
\delta_4(h)=\sqrt{\lambda^2-h^2}/\lambda-\sqrt{1-h^2}.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: For positive density this equals \(D(h)\), including at the curvature endpoint one.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the normalized four-arc scalar area
\[
2[B(h)+h\delta_4(h)]/h^2.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The scalar-identification theorem equates it to \(A_4(h)\) on the stated domain.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the four-arc scalar perimeter
\[
4B(h)/h.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This already agrees definitionally with the article's perimeter expression.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every real \(h\), the function
\[
q(h)=2h-1
\]
has derivative two.
classifications.latex_explanation: This is the affine chain-rule factor in the three-arc angle and radical derivatives.

classifications.informal_statement:
For \(\lambda>1\) and \(0<h<1\), the three-arc angle combination has derivative
\[
2[1/\sqrt{1-q(h)^2}-\lambda/\sqrt{\lambda^2-q(h)^2}].
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: Differentiate the inverse trigonometric functions and include the affine factor two. Both radical denominators are positive.

classifications.informal_statement:
For \(\lambda>1\) and \(0<h<1\), \(\delta_3\) has derivative
\[
2q(h)[1/\sqrt{1-q(h)^2}-1/(\lambda\sqrt{\lambda^2-q(h)^2})].
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The derivative of each normalized radical is legitimate in the open parameter interval; no endpoint derivative is asserted.

classifications.informal_statement: For \(\lambda>1\) and \(0<h<1\), the normalized three-arc area is differentiable at \(h\), and its perimeter has derivative \(h\) times that area derivative.
classifications.latex_explanation: The proof differentiates the two explicit quotients and cancels their difference by the radical identity. It is a local variational result, not a global monotonicity theorem.

classifications.informal_statement:
For \(\lambda>1\), the normalized three-arc area tends to
\[
+\infty
\]
as \(h\downarrow0\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
The numerator tends to
\[
\lambda\arccos(-1/\lambda)+\sqrt{\lambda^2-1}/\lambda>0.
\]
A positive lower numerator bound and a diverging reciprocal imply the result.

classifications.informal_statement:
For real \(\theta\), define
\[
\ell(\theta)=\theta/\sin\theta.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(0<\theta<\pi\), this is the circular arc length normalized by chord length; the definition is total outside that interval as well.

classifications.informal_statement:
For real \(\theta\), define
\[
a(\theta)=(\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta)/(4\sin^2\theta).
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: For \(0<\theta<\pi\), this is the area of the circular segment with unit chord and half-central-angle \(\theta\), including major segments.

classifications.informal_statement:
For \(0<\theta<\pi\), the normalized segment area satisfies
\[
a(\theta)>0.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The numerator is strictly positive on this interval and the squared sine denominator is positive; scaling by a positive chord square gives positive cap area.

classifications.informal_statement:
A three-arc assembly consists of real \(\lambda,h\) with \(\lambda>1\) and
\[
0<h<1.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
All other geometric data are determined by these parameters. Throughout these entries use
\[
R=1/h,
\]

\[
q=2h-1,
\]

\[
\beta=\arccos q,
\]

\[
\alpha=\arccos(q/\lambda),
\]

\[
\phi=\pi-\beta,
\]
and
\[
b=R(\sin\alpha-\sin\beta).
\]

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
R=1/h.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The admissible curvature is strictly between zero and one, so the radius is greater than one.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
q=2h-1.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This affine shape parameter belongs to \((-1,1)\) on the assembly domain.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
\beta=\arccos q.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This angle locates the inner circle's top intersection; the exposed side-arc angle is its supplement.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the outer inverse-cosine argument
\[
q/\lambda.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The density contrast rescales the inner cosine through the incidence relation.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
\alpha=\arccos(q/\lambda).
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The full principal angle interval \((0,\pi)\) permits both minor and major exterior caps.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
\phi=\pi-\beta.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: Each strip arc turns through \(\phi\), while the auxiliary symmetric side cap has central angle \(2\phi\).

classifications.informal_statement:
Define
\[
b=R(\sin\alpha-\sin\beta).
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
It is the half-length of the exposed bottom segment and equals
\[
D(q)/h.
\]

classifications.informal_statement: Define the left circle center \((-b,R-1)\).
classifications.latex_explanation: Its lowest point has height minus one, providing tangency to the bottom interface.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the right circle center \((b,R-1)\).
classifications.latex_explanation: It is the vertical-axis reflection of the left center.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the upper circle center \((0,1-R\cos\alpha)\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
Its intersections with the top interface have half-chord

R\sin\alpha.

Define the rectangle

\{(x,y):-b\leq x\leq b,\ -1\leq y\leq1\}.

classifications.latex_explanation: The rectangle may have zero width when \(h=1/2\); the overall carrier is still a disk there.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the radius-\(R\) disk centered at \((-b,R-1)\), clipped by

x\leq-b

and

-1\leq y\leq1.

classifications.latex_explanation: This is the left part of the strip core outside its central rectangle.

classifications.informal_statement:

\[
x\geq b

and

-1\leq y\leq1.

classifications.latex_explanation: The right clipped disk is the reflection of the left one.

classifications.latex_explanation: Its horizontal-section description is later identified with the literal three-arc core inequality.

classifications.informal_statement:
The left trace consists of points on the circle centered at \((-b,R-1)\) with radius \(R\), satisfying

x\leq-b

and

-1\leq y\leq1.

The right trace consists of points on the circle centered at \((b,R-1)\) with radius \(R\), satisfying

x\geq b

and
\[
-1\leq y\leq1.

classifications.latex_explanation: It includes the top and bottom endpoints of the exposed right arc.

Define the left arclength parametrization

s\mapsto(-b+R\sin(s/R),R-1-R\cos(s/R)).

classifications.latex_explanation: The selected parameter interval is \([-R\phi,0]\), ending at the bottom tangency point.

s\mapsto(b+R\sin(s/R),R-1-R\cos(s/R)).

classifications.latex_explanation: The selected parameter interval is \([0,R\phi]\), starting at the bottom tangency point.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the bottom segment
\[
\{(x,-1):|x|\leq b\}.

classifications.latex_explanation: It is retained also for \(b=0\), when it is a singleton rather than an empty set.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the bottom chord length as \(2b\).
classifications.latex_explanation: The construction allows this nonnegative length to vanish at the semicircular parameter.

classifications.informal_statement:
Every admissible three-arc assembly has
\[
R>0.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: Its curvature is positive, so its reciprocal is positive.

classifications.informal_statement:
Every admissible three-arc assembly has
\[
R>1.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The strict upper curvature bound makes the reciprocal strictly greater than one, ensuring a regular three-arc core.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
-1<q<1.

classifications.latex_explanation:
This follows directly from \(0<h<1\) and
\[
q=2h-1.
\]

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

-1<q/\lambda<1.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The positive density contrast exceeds one, so rescaling preserves strict containment in the inverse-cosine domain.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

\beta>0.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

For every assembly,

\alpha>0.

For every assembly,
\[
\alpha<\pi.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
\cos\beta=q.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The inverse cosine is evaluated within its valid argument interval.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
\cos\alpha=q/\lambda.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This realizes the prescribed refraction relation in cosine coordinates.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

Rh=1.

classifications.latex_explanation: Cancel the positive curvature in the reciprocal radius.

For every assembly,

\sin\alpha>0.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

classifications.informal_statement:

\phi>0.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,

\phi<\pi.

classifications.latex_explanation: The inner angle is strictly positive.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
\sin\phi=\sin\beta.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: Sine is unchanged under supplementation.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
\cos\phi=-q.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
Cosine changes sign under supplementation, and
\[
\cos\beta=q.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the auxiliary lower cap with chord
\[
2R\sin\beta,

half-angle \(\phi\), midpoint \((0,1)\), and lower orientation.
classifications.latex_explanation: Its area equals the sum of the two translated side pieces. It is a calculation device, not an additional exterior cap in the competitor.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the upper cap with chord
\[
2R\sin\alpha,
\]
half-angle \(\alpha\), midpoint \((0,1)\), and upper orientation.
classifications.latex_explanation: Its radius is proved to be \(R\), and its actual carrier completes the competitor above the strip.

classifications.informal_statement: The three-arc carrier is its strip core union its upper cap.
classifications.latex_explanation: The bottom segment is part of its frontier, not a separate area-bearing component.

classifications.informal_statement: The assembly weighted area is the Lebesgue weighted-area integral over its actual carrier.
classifications.latex_explanation: It is distinct by definition from the modeled scalar sum, which is identified by a theorem.

classifications.informal_statement: The assembly weighted perimeter is the density integral against the canonical complete-frontier measure of its carrier.
classifications.latex_explanation: Unlike the auxiliary four-arc parametrized perimeter, this definition starts directly with the geometric frontier.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the scalar rectangle area as \(4b\).
classifications.latex_explanation: The height is two and the width is \(2b\); the formula includes zero width.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the modeled weighted area as \(4b\) plus the auxiliary side-cap area plus \(\lambda\) times the outer-cap area.
classifications.latex_explanation: This scalar decomposition is proved to agree with the actual carrier integral; it is not an extra hypothesis.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the modeled perimeter as the auxiliary side-cap arc length plus \(\lambda\) times the outer-cap arc length plus \(2b\).
classifications.latex_explanation: The last term is the density-one bottom segment, and the side-cap arc length equals the total length of the two strip arcs.

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the angle combination
\[
T=\lambda\alpha+\pi-\beta.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
Using
\[
\pi-\arccos q=\pi/2+\arcsin q,
\]
this equals
\[
B(q)+\pi/2.
\]

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the sine gap
\[
\delta=\sin\alpha-\sin\beta.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
The coordinate bridge identifies it with \(D(q)\), and the side half-width is
\[
R\delta.
\]

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the scalar area
\[
[T+(q+2)\delta]/h^2.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: After the angle and sine identifications, this is exactly the article's \(A_3(h)\).

classifications.informal_statement:
Define the scalar perimeter
\[
2(T+\delta)/h.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: This is the article's \(P_3(h)\), including the exposed bottom segment.

classifications.informal_statement:
For every assembly,
\[
\sin\beta\leq\sin\alpha.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
Compare
\[
\sqrt{1-q^2}
\]
and
\[
\sqrt{1-q^2/\lambda^2},
\]
using \(\lambda>1\).

classifications.informal_statement:
If an assembly has
\[
h\ne1/2,
\]
then
\[
\sin\beta<\sin\alpha.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation:
Then \(q\ne0\), so rescaling its square by
\[
\lambda^2>1
\]
gives a strict radical comparison.

classifications.informal_statement: For every assembly, \(b\geq0\).
classifications.latex_explanation: It is the positive radius times a nonnegative sine gap.
Use strict positivity of the sine gap away from the zero shape parameter.

classifications.informal_statement:
For an admissible assembly,
\[
b=0
\]
if and only if \(h=1/2\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
At one half both angles are
\[
\pi/2;
\]
away from one half the gap is strictly positive.

classifications.informal_statement: For every assembly, the bottom chord length \(2b\) is nonnegative.
classifications.latex_explanation: This permits a degenerate segment without excluding the disk case.

classifications.informal_statement: The bottom chord has zero length if and only if \(h=1/2\).
classifications.latex_explanation: Its length is twice the side half-width, whose exact zero locus was proved.

classifications.informal_statement: If \(h\ne1/2\), the bottom chord has strictly positive length.
classifications.latex_explanation: The positive factor two preserves strict positivity of the side half-width.

classifications.informal_statement:
If \(h=1/2\), the inner angle is
\[
\beta=\pi/2.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The shape parameter vanishes, so its inverse cosine is the right angle.

classifications.informal_statement:
If \(h=1/2\), the outer half-angle is
\[
\alpha=\pi/2.
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: The outer argument also vanishes for the positive density parameter.

classifications.informal_statement: The constructed outer cap has radius \(R\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
Its chord is
\[
2R\sin\alpha;
\]
cancellation in the cap-radius definition proves the identity.

classifications.informal_statement: The auxiliary side cap has radius \(R\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
Its chord uses
\[
\sin\beta=\sin\phi,
\]
which cancels the sine of its cap half-angle.

classifications.informal_statement: The auxiliary side cap has center \((0,R-1)\).
classifications.latex_explanation:
For its lower orientation the center height is
\[
1+R\cos\phi=1-Rq=R-1,
\]
using
\[
Rh=1.
\]

classifications.informal_statement: The left arc parametrization maps \([-R\phi,0]\) exactly onto the left coordinate arc trace.
classifications.latex_explanation: The circle and strip constraints give one inclusion; inverse trigonometric reconstruction on the declared arc gives the reverse inclusion.

classifications.informal_statement: The right arc parametrization maps \([0,R\phi]\) exactly onto the right coordinate arc trace.
classifications.latex_explanation: The circle and strip constraints give one inclusion; inverse trigonometric reconstruction on the declared arc gives the reverse inclusion.

classifications.informal_statement:
For any planar center \(c\), define the complex-to-Euclidean map
\[
z\mapsto(c_x+\operatorname{Im}z,c_y-\operatorname{Re}z).
\]
classifications.latex_explanation: It carries the standard circle to a circle centered at \(c\), with the orientation used for the inner arcs.

classifications.informal_statement: For every center \(c\), the side-arc complex map is an isometry.
classifications.latex_explanation: A coordinate interchange, sign change and translation preserve the Euclidean metric.

classifications.informal_statement: Define the realized left arc parametrization by applying the Euclidean coordinate homeomorphism to its coordinate parametrization.
classifications.latex_explanation: This makes the Euclidean metric explicit without altering the point set.
